title: Form Validator
story: Your team just launched a sign-up page, but the backend keeps crashing on bad input — empty names, ages like 'banana', and emails without the @ sign. You decide to build a bulletproof form validator that checks every field and returns the FIRST specific error found, so the user knows exactly what to fix.
why: Validating multiple fields sequentially with Result teaches the guard-clause pattern — fail fast with a precise error message, and only return success when every check passes.
analogy: A form validator is like a security checkpoint at an airport. The first station checks your ID (name). If it's blank, you don't get to the metal detector. If your ID is good, you move to baggage scan (age — must be parseable and in range). If your bag is suspicious, you're stopped there. Only when all three stations clear you do you get the green light to board.
try_it: Test each field failing individually: empty name, 'banana' as age, age 999, email without @. Then add a fourth field: 'username' must be at least 3 characters AND contain no spaces. Add a fifth field: 'password' must be at least 8 characters. Chain all 5 validations. Does the order of checks affect which error the user sees first?
tips: Check the cheapest validations first (like empty string) — no point parsing a number if the name is blank
Guard clauses keep code flat: each `if bad { return Err(...) }` avoids nested if-else pyramids
The `match` on `string.str_to_int` handles BOTH parse failure AND range checking in one block
common_mistakes: Checking email before name — if the user fixes their name, they still have to wait for the email error
Using `?` on `string.str_to_int` without a custom message — the default parse error might be confusing to end users
Forgetting that `string.str_contains` is case-sensitive — `Email@` and `email@` are valid but `EMAIL@` still passes
